title: 70 Solar grazing schools create opportunity for sheep production in solar arrays
content:
Abstract
Growth in solar energy production has created opportunity to use sheep to manage the vegetation in these sites. Healthy vegetation and healthy soil under the solar array is desirable to prevent soil erosion, but plant height must be controlled to prevent shading and to stop plants from touching the underside of the panels. Vegetation management is usually accomplished with frequent mowing which is both expensive and counterproductive to reducing greenhouse gas emissions through green energy. Finding suitable grazing land is often difficult when starting or expanding a sheep enterprise. The opportunity for additional pasture and attractive payments for solar array vegetation management services have drawn the interest of veteran shepherds and entrepreneurs new to sheep production. However, securing a vegetation management contract is complicated, and both training and patience are required. In May 2024, the American Lamb Board with support from North Carolina State Extension and Amazing Grazing presented two solar grazing schools. The locations were Roxboro, NC and Temple, TX. These states have shown tremendous growth in the number of solar installations (NC=55,072; TX=279,434) [AW1] with TX ranking first nationally. Growth potential of the next five years shows a dramatic increase for TX and lower gains in NC (NC=Rank 26th; TX=Rank 1st nationally). Both schools were certified through the American Solar Grazing Association and met associated curriculum requirements. Both schools included classroom and field training. Topics included pasture ecology, grazing management, marketing, sheep production, securing a solar grazing contract and working with solar companies. Most attendees were from the school’s host state (NC=41.6%; TX=73.5%) with total attendance of 24 and 34 for NC and TX, respectively. States bordering the host state showed good attendance[AW2]. Attendees who raised sheep had been doing so for approximately 7 years for both schools. Total sheep numbers raised varied greatly by location (NC=1,860; TX=36,593) with average flock size following a similar pattern (NC=124; TX=1,219). Attendees were ask if they currently provide grazing services. NC had only one producer actively grazing solar arrays with 121 ha under management. Thirteen TX producers who attended the TX school provide vegetation management services on 9,606 ha with an average size of 738 ha. Five TX producers indicated that they would start offering grazing services within six months. The demand for electricity continues to grow and solar arrays are going to be part of our landscapes. Solar grazing provides opportunities and unique challenges. More research and education is need to develop and implement best management practices to address this system. Demand for training in this area will continue to grow with greater adoption of solar grazing.
